title: Alcaraz Loses at 3:34 A.M., Walks Off Smiling: 'I Suffered, But I Enjoyed'
summary:
Most tennis players would not smile after losing a five-set match at 3:34 in the morning. Carlos Alcaraz is not most players.

After his US Open title defense ended against Ben Shelton — a grueling four-hour, 28-minute battle — the 23-year-old Spaniard was filmed walking down the Arthur Ashe tunnel with a huge grin. It was the latest finish in the tournament's history.

Why the smile? Alcaraz had been out for over five months with a wrist injury that left him in pain every day. He missed the French Open and Wimbledon. He didn't know if he'd even play in New York until a week before.

"I suffered, but I enjoyed and that's why I smiled when I walked out of the court because I missed that feeling," he said.

The late finish wasn't unusual at this US Open. Eventual champion Alexander Zverev finished past 1 a.m. in three of his first five matches. Venus Williams finished her first-round match at 2 a.m.

"I think it's too much," Alcaraz said of the schedule. "The last match people stayed but if that match was played earlier, the court could have been packed." He suggested a maximum finish time of 11 p.m.

Alcaraz isn't the only player who missed big chunks of the season. Britain's Jack Draper struggled with an arm injury and ended his season early. Alcaraz's rival Jannik Sinner missed the US Open with a knee injury. Alcaraz said he'll skip some tournaments in the future to stay "mentally and physically healthy."

This week, he's competing for Team Europe in the Laver Cup at The O2 in London, captained by Yannick Noah against a World team led by Andre Agassi.

"When you have your team-mates, the best in the world, by your side, it's a weird feeling but it's beautiful," he said. "We played like our lives depend on it."
why_it_matters: The 3:34 a.m. finish exposes a structural conflict in professional sport: tournaments earn huge money from late-night television slots, but players' bodies and recovery are treated as the cost — and Alcaraz's decision to skip events may push a new generation of athletes to protect their health over their ranking.

background_read: The US Open is one of tennis's four Grand Slam tournaments, alongside the Australian Open, the French Open and Wimbledon. It is played in New York at Arthur Ashe Stadium, the largest tennis stadium in the world, and its night sessions have a long history of running past midnight — a complaint players have raised for years.

Carlos Alcaraz is a Spanish player who became the youngest world No. 1 in the sport's history after winning the 2022 US Open as a teenager. Ben Shelton, the opponent who beat him here, is a young American left-hander known for one of the fastest serves on tour.

The Laver Cup is an annual team event named after Rod Laver, the Australian champion widely considered one of the greatest players ever. It pits a team of European players against a 'World' team and was launched with the backing of Roger Federer, who helped turn it into a regular stop on the calendar.

OPEN QUESTION: Will the sport ever change a schedule built around late-night television?

perspectives.description: Historic late-night matches create unforgettable drama and huge audiences, and Alcaraz's grace in defeat gave the sport a rare, likeable moment. His honesty about enjoying competition again after five months out is exactly the attitude organisers want to promote.

Finishing a four-and-a-half-hour match at 3:34 a.m. leaves no room for proper recovery, and the tournament's schedule prioritises ticket sales and television over athletes' bodies. With several top players out with injuries, the calendar itself looks like part of the problem.

Late finishes are an old issue, not a one-off: night sessions sell the most expensive tickets and deliver prime-time advertising, so tournaments have little incentive to move them. Changing it would require the Grand Slams, tours and broadcasters to agree together, which is exactly why it has rarely happened.

Alcaraz's suggested 11 p.m. cut-off has been raised by other players before, and shorter formats or earlier starts are possible if stars keep speaking out. His own plan to skip tournaments also hints at a shift in which top players treat a long career as more valuable than a packed schedule.
